titleText.es: Hay un montón de licenciados entre los creacionistas de la Tierra Joven
titleText.en: There are a lot of college-educated young-Earth creationists.
titleText.noteEn: Licenciados here means people with university degrees; the title text comments on the education level of one group named in the comic.

regions.labelEs: LA HISTORIA OFICIAL DEL 11-S ESTÁ LLENA DE AGUJEROS. MIRA POR EJEMPLO...

applications.explanationEn: Está gives the current state, llena matches the feminine noun historia, and de introduces what fills it.
Por ejemplo signals that a specific example is about to follow.

regions.labelEs: PARA, POR FAVOR, PORQUE VER QUE TE PASA ESTO A TI ME PARTE EL CORAZÓN.

applications.explanationEn: Por favor makes the request to stop more polite.
Te already identifies the affected person, while a ti repeats that person for emphasis.
Me marks whose heart is affected, and parte el corazón supplies the fixed image of heartbreak.

regions.labelEs: LAS TEORÍAS DE LA CONSPIRACIÓN REPRESENTAN UN FALLO CONOCIDO DEL RAZONAMIENTO HUMANO. POR SUPUESTO, A VECES ESTAS TEORÍAS SON VERDADERAS, PERO SU VERDAD NO TIENE ABSOLUTAMENTE NINGUNA CORRELACIÓN CON LA CERTEZA DEL CREYENTE. POR ALGUNA RAZÓN, A VECES, CUANDO LA GENTE CREE QUE HA DESTAPADO UNA MENTIRA, ELEVAN EL SESGO DE CONFIRMACIÓN A UNA FORMA DE ARTE. RETIRAN EL CONTEXTO DE LOS HECHOS Y LOS ARGUMENTOS Y LOS CONVIERTEN EN LETANÍAS TRANQUILIZADORAS. UNA Y OTRA VEZ HE DISCUTIDO EN VANO CON PERSONAS INTELIGENTES CONSUMIDAS POR TEORÍAS QUE PENSABAN IRREFUTABLES Y QUE AL FINAL DEMOSTRARON SER COMPLETAS FICCIONES.

applications.explanationEn: Teorías is plural, while de la conspiración stays unchanged as the type of theory.
Por supuesto acknowledges that the following concession is obvious or expected.
A veces limits the claim to some occasions rather than all occasions.
No stays before tiene even though ninguna supplies a second negative after the verb.
Tiene supplies the form of tener, and correlación con names the relationship being denied.
Por alguna razón introduces a cause that the speaker cannot explain.
A veces again marks the behavior as occasional rather than universal.
Ha is the present form of haber for one person or thing, and destapado is the completed-action form that follows it.

applications.exampleEs: ELEVAN EL SESGO DE CONFIRMACIÓN A UNA FORMA DE ARTE
applications.explanationEn: Elevan names the figurative raising, the middle words identify the activity, and a una forma de arte gives the exaggerated result.
Los stands for the facts and arguments, convierten gives the action, and en introduces what they become.
Una y otra vez emphasizes that the arguing happened repeatedly.
He marks the speaker, and discutido is the unchanged completed-action form after it.
En vano says the repeated discussions did not achieve their intended result.
Que stands for the theories being judged, and irrefutables states what the people considered them to be.
Al final introduces the eventual outcome after the beliefs were examined.
Demostraron ser presents the later outcome, and completas ficciones names what the theories proved to be.

regions.labelEs: LOS CREACIONISTAS DE LA TIERRA JOVEN, LOS DEL ALUNIZAJE, LA SUBCULTURA DEL MOVIMIENTO PERPETUO... ¿NO VES QUE ESTÁS CAYENDO EN EL MISMO PATRÓN?

applications.explanationEn: Estás identifies informal singular you, and cayendo presents the fall as in progress.
Cayendo en is figurative here, and el mismo patrón names the repeated way of reasoning.

regions.labelEs: NO CREES EN SERIO QUE HEMOS ATERRIZADO EN LA LUNA, ¿VERDAD?

applications.explanationEn: En serio questions whether the belief is genuine, not whether it is solemn.
Hemos marks we, and aterrizado is the completed-action form that follows it.
Verdad at the end asks the listener to confirm the preceding claim.
Dios mío is both an exclamation and, in this scene, a literal address to God.
Dime combines the informal command di with the attached pronoun me.
Mío follows hijo and matches its masculine singular form.

regions.labelEs: QUIERO ABRIR UN INFORME DE ERROR.

applications.explanationEn: Abrir means creating the report, and informe de error names the software issue record.

cards.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.

example.en: I’m coming from the market.

cards.answerEn: the Spanish abbreviation for the September 11, 2001 attacks
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly names major dated events with the day number and the month initial. 11-S corresponds to English 9/11 because Spanish puts the day before the month.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is full of something else?
cards.answerEn: Use estar, then lleno or llena, then de.
cards.noteEn: Change lleno to match the thing that is full: lleno for a masculine singular noun and llena for a feminine singular noun. The thing filling it follows de.

example.es: La caja está llena de libros.
example.en: The box is full of books.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por ejemplo (“for example”)

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce an example?
cards.noteEn: Por ejemplo works like English “for example” or “for instance.” It can introduce an example before or after a complete statement.

example.es: Me gustan muchos deportes, por ejemplo, el tenis.
example.en: I like many sports—for example, tennis.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por favor (“please”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “please”?
cards.noteEn: Por favor makes a request more polite. It can appear before or after the request.

example.en: Close the door, please.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.en: I’m sending you a message.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens to a particular person?
cards.answerEn: Name what happens, and put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before a changed form of pasar to identify the affected person. You may also name that person after the Spanish word a.
cards.noteEn: Pasar changes to match the thing or event that happens, not the affected person: esto me pasa but estas cosas me pasan. With the verb's unchanged dictionary form, attach the short pronoun to the end: pasarle. In the prompt, algo stands for what happens and alguien for the affected person; those words do not have to appear literally. Spanish may repeat the affected person after a, a word often translated as ‘to,’ for clarity or emphasis, while English normally states the person once.

example.es: Eso me pasó a mí ayer.
example.en: That happened to me yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something breaks someone’s heart?
cards.answerEn: Use partirle el corazón a alguien.
cards.noteEn: The short pronoun identifies the person affected: me parte el corazón means “it breaks my heart,” and te parte el corazón means “it breaks your heart.”

example.es: La noticia le partió el corazón.
example.en: The news broke her heart.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “conspiracy theory”?
cards.answerEn: Use teoría de la conspiración; the plural is teorías de la conspiración.
cards.noteEn: The linking word de stays between teoría and la conspiración. Only teoría changes to teorías in the plural.

example.es: Esa teoría de la conspiración no tiene pruebas.
example.en: That conspiracy theory has no evidence.

cards.promptEs: informe de error aplicado al razonamiento humano
cards.answerEn: treating a flaw in human reasoning as if it were a software bug
cards.noteEn: A software user files a bug report so a defect can be fixed. The metaphor applies that technical workflow to an undesirable feature of the human mind.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “of course” when something is obvious or agreed?
cards.noteEn: Por supuesto is a fixed expression. It can confirm a request or emphasize that the speaker sees something as expected.

example.en: Of course, you can come in.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)
no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.

example.en: Sometimes I cook at home.

cards.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

example.en: I tried it three times.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is correlated with another?
cards.noteEn: Use the appropriate form of tener, followed by correlación con and the other quantity or fact.

example.es: El resultado tiene correlación con la edad.
example.en: The result is correlated with age.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “for some reason”?
cards.noteEn: This expression introduces a cause that the speaker does not know or does not explain.

example.es: Por alguna razón, la puerta no abre.
example.en: For some reason, the door will not open.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.promptEs: elevar algo a una forma de arte
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes an activity to the level of an art form?
cards.answerEn: Use elevar algo a una forma de arte.
cards.noteEn: This is often humorous or critical. It says someone does an activity with such intensity or skill that it resembles an art form.

example.es: Elevó la procrastinación a una forma de arte.
example.en: He turned procrastination into an art form.

cards.answerEn: the tendency to favor evidence that supports what one already believes
cards.noteEn: Confirmation bias can make people seek, remember, or interpret information in ways that protect an existing belief while discounting contrary evidence.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone turns one thing into another?
cards.answerEn: Use convertir, name the thing being changed, then en and the result.
cards.noteEn: The form of convertir changes with the person and time. En introduces what the original thing becomes.

example.es: Convirtieron el garaje en una oficina.
example.en: They turned the garage into an office.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “over and over” or “again and again”?
cards.noteEn: The expression emphasizes that the same event or action happens repeatedly.

example.es: Leyó el mensaje una y otra vez.
example.en: She read the message over and over.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an effort was unsuccessful or pointless?
cards.noteEn: En vano means the effort did not achieve its intended result, like English “in vain.”

example.en: I tried to convince him in vain.

cards.questionEn: How can pensar describe what someone considers a thing to be?
cards.answerEn: Use pensar, the thing being judged, and an adjective describing that judgment.
cards.noteEn: Here pensar means “to consider” rather than simply “to think.” A relative word such as que can stand for the thing being judged.

example.en: They considered the plan impossible.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: in the; part of al final (“in the end”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “in the end” or “eventually”?
cards.noteEn: Al final can name the literal end of something or the eventual outcome after events have unfolded.

example.en: In the end, we decided to stay.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something ultimately proves or turns out to have a quality?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of demostrar followed by ser and the description.
cards.noteEn: In this pattern, demostrar does not mean that the subject presents a proof. It says later evidence showed what the subject really was.

example.en: The decision proved to be correct.

cards.answerEn: the belief that Earth and life were created only thousands of years ago
cards.noteEn: Young-Earth creationism rejects the much older age of Earth supported by modern geology, astronomy, and evolutionary biology.

cards.answerEn: the conspiracy claim that the Apollo Moon landings did not happen
cards.noteEn: Moon-landing denial claims that NASA staged the Apollo landings despite extensive physical, photographic, technical, and independent evidence for the missions.

cards.answerEn: hypothetical motion that continues forever without an energy source
cards.noteEn: A machine that produces useful work forever without added energy would violate the laws of thermodynamics. Claims of such machines are therefore treated as impossible under established physics.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

example.en: I am reading.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone falls into the same pattern?
cards.answerEn: Use caer en el mismo patrón.
cards.noteEn: Caer en can describe entering a repeated mistake or way of behaving, not only physically falling into a place.

example.es: Volvimos a caer en el mismo patrón.
example.en: We fell into the same pattern again.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)

cards.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cards.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cards.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cards.questionEn: How do you add “right?” or “isn’t that so?” to check agreement?
cards.noteEn: Verdad literally means “truth,” but at the end of a statement it asks the listener to confirm the claim.

example.en: You are coming tomorrow, right?

cards.questionEn: How do you exclaim “my God”?
cards.noteEn: Dios mío can express shock, frustration, or a literal address to God. Mío follows Dios and agrees with its masculine form.

example.en: My God! What happened?

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

example.en: Sit down here!

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish say “my” or “your” after the noun instead of before it?
cards.answerEn: Put mío, mía, tuyo, or tuya after the noun and match the noun’s gender and number.
cards.noteEn: This form is common in addresses and relationships such as hijo mío and amiga mía. Unlike mi or tu before a noun, the longer form changes to match the noun.

example.en: My friend, listen.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “to file or open a bug report”?
cards.answerEn: Use abrir un informe de error.
cards.noteEn: In software, informe de error means a report describing a bug. Abrir means creating or filing that report in a tracking system.

example.es: Voy a abrir un informe de error.
example.en: I am going to file a bug report.
